Sample.evidence_source: [page/8/3] We recognise that in this retrospective study, our narrative data represent reconstructions of the SCE 'as told' by participants, rather than being objective accounts of the event 'as lived'.

Population.evidence_source: [page/8/3] This study is limited to completed suicides but it may also be appropriate to investigate SCEs in a broader sample, including the social networks of those who have survived suicide attempts.

Type.evidence_source: [page/8/2] However, as previously reported (Owens et al., 2011), our data show that, notwithstanding their desire to help, lay people are often unsure how to intervene in a suicidal crisis.

Area.evidence_source: [page/7/5] Our data demonstrate that SCEs can be highly face-threatening situations that are managed using face-saving tactics, including humour and off-record strategies such as strategic ambiguity and euphemistic talk. [page/7/5] Yet when the speaker bypasses face-saving using a direct commissive suicide speech act, our data show that it can be the listener who mitigates the illocutionary force of the utterance by misinterpreting its sincerity. [page/7/6] Whereas Wolk-Wasserman (1986) found that the majority of family members understood the suicidal communication but were ambivalent about helping, we found that difficulties in responding to SCEs were more frequently presented as pragmatic failures to correctly determine the meaning of the communication. [page/8/2] Lack of knowledge and confidence about intervening could make people even more reluctant to acknowledge and explore the frightening implications of what is meant by what is said. [page/8/2] Furthermore, fear of damaging a personal relationship by reading a SCE as sincere and responding inappropriately (in itself a potentially face-threatening act) may have led our participants to avoid such interpretations. [page/8/2] Mutual face-work in SCEs may sometimes be about relieving and avoiding the obligation to intervene when both interlocutors are ambivalent, fearful and unsure what to do.
